title: The advertised number and the governing one

turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Friday, the twenty-fifth of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three things. A Chinese state visit to Washington, the first in eleven years — twenty-one guns, a state dinner, and no joint statement.
[curious] None at all? We checked?
We read the White House page directly. Nothing. Second: gold fell during a shooting war.
Which sounds impossible until you hear why. And the third?
A hobby where you buy a stone and then deliberately destroy three-quarters of it.
[amused] That one's mine. Hold it.
Washington first. Xi Jinping and Peng Liyuan landed at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday, and Trump and the First Lady met them at the foot of the airstairs.
At the airstairs? That isn't normal.
Xinhua called it a rare planeside welcome. Agence France-Presse said it was the first such greeting by an American president in more than sixty years.
[thoughtful] Sixty. So what came out of it?
A paragraph. A two-month extension of the trade truce, which was due to expire on the tenth of November. Rare-earth restrictions deferred to the tenth of January.
And the tariffs themselves?
Untouched. Thirty-six and a half per cent American on Chinese goods, thirty-one per cent the other way. Plus a hundred thousand student places, and two pandas for Atlanta.
[chuckles] Pandas. But genuinely no communiqué?
Our desk read the briefings page for the twenty-first to the twenty-fourth. The only China items were the First Lady's dinner details and a Smithsonian visit.
[pause] So the absence is the document.

That's how we wrote it. Xinhua listed areas of cooperation rather than agreements — foreign affairs, finance, law enforcement, artificial-intelligence governance, direct flights, military crisis channels.
Areas, not agreements. What did the room outside make of it?
Al Jazeera quoted the analyst Einar Tangen calling it transactional theatre — election optics, not substance. The warmest read available was a useful interim step.
[skeptical] And we've seen this film before.
The January twenty-twenty Phase One deal committed China to two hundred billion dollars of extra American goods over two years. It fell far short.
Anyone put that well?
Jim Sutter of the US Soybean Export Council, this week: even after a big signing ceremony, it didn't really live up to what we had hoped.
Ouch. And the current pledge?

Already half-empty. Beijing was said at Busan to have agreed twenty-five million tonnes of American soybeans a year. Analysts put it halfway to this year's number, and Beijing has never publicly confirmed the figure.
[deadpan] So what did the sixty days actually buy?

Predictability for the electronics supply chain — which happens to be the one thing standing between Singapore's export boom and a very different fourth quarter. The weapon wasn't disarmed. It was deferred.
[thoughtful] And it expires four weeks before Chinese New Year.

It does. Meanwhile, around eighty countries signed a statement at the United Nations demanding the Strait of Hormuz be reopened. Still shut. And Iran has opened a new front — airports. Its security-council secretary warned that any country cooperating with the United States would lose its flights to Iran. Azerbaijan and Georgia suspended Iranian flights on Wednesday, the Emirates on Thursday. Iran's own international capacity was down forty-nine per cent year-on-year in August.
And the regional cost?
Near six hundred million US dollars a day in lost visitor spending — though one analyst thinks strikes on airports themselves are extremely unlikely.
Good. And Ethiopia? I saw something about Tigray.

Back to war. Twenty-one airstrikes reported on the twenty-second, two on schools in Alamata, at least fourteen dead. By the twenty-third the TPLF had seized three airports and the national airline suspended all flights there.
[sighs] After everything. The last war killed how many?
Roughly six hundred thousand.
All right. The money block. You promised me gold falling during a war.

Start at the end of the chain, because that's where it gives itself away. Brent rose about four per cent on Thursday to roughly a hundred and seven dollars, Hormuz is disrupted — and gold fell three-tenths of a per cent.
[curious] That's backwards.

To four thousand two hundred and seventy-four dollars, down more than eight per cent on the month. Two things are outbidding fear: the real yield, and the dollar. Three central banks raised rates within nine days. The Federal Reserve on the sixteenth — a quarter point, unanimously, its first rise since twenty twenty-three. The European Central Bank on the tenth. The Bank of Japan on the eighteenth, to its highest since nineteen ninety-five. None of them. Then Thursday's data came in hot — the American flash composite index at fifty-eight point four, the strongest private-sector expansion since July twenty twenty-one.
And the bond market?
Broke first. A weak five-year auction left dealers holding paper, and on Thursday the ten-year jumped nine basis points to five point two one per cent — the highest since two thousand and seven.
[exhales] Two thousand and seven. So what do you call this regime?
Higher-for-longer, dollar-bid, and a supply shock being fought with demand tools. It is not risk-off — equities were flat, not broken, because nominal growth is genuinely strong.
And for someone holding an all-world fund and global bonds?
That's the uncomfortable part. Both legs lost on the same day. That's the signature of a rates shock, not a growth scare — diversification isn't helping this week.
And bitcoin?
Eighty-four thousand, barely moved. Behaving as a liquidity proxy in a tightening. Quiet, not safe. And none of this is advice.
Is anyone arguing the Fed has this wrong?
Yes, and it's the sharpest line in the issue. From the South Shore Press: raising interest rates doesn't unclog a pipeline or reroute a tanker. It just makes it more expensive to borrow money.
[laughs] Well, quite.

Goldman's economists argued the September case was weak, while putting twelve-month recession odds near fifteen per cent. Core inflation hit two point two per cent in August — highest in about two years. Electricity and gas running at eight point seven.
Because of the tariff, which rose how much?
Seventeen per cent in July, to thirty-one point nine one cents a kilowatt-hour. About seventeen dollars a month on a four-room flat. And the next announcement lands around Monday.
What did they say last time?
That if the situation improved, fourth-quarter tariffs may decrease.
[skeptical] Has the situation improved?

No. The tariff tracks imported gas indexed to oil with a lag of about two and a half months, so the fourth-quarter window runs mid-July to mid-September. Brent was up fifty-six per cent year-on-year. No cut on Monday. And we printed three ways we could be wrong, because that's our inference from the published mechanism, not a sourced forecast.
That's fair. Anything else local?

Exports rose forty-six point two per cent in August, the fastest since nineteen eighty-eight. And forty-five per cent of forecasters now expect the central bank to tighten its currency band in October.
Booming exports, rising prices — and the index?
Fell anyway. A rates day, not a Singapore day.
Technology. What happened in Hangzhou?

Alibaba announced an entire Chinese artificial-intelligence stack. Its chip arm unveiled a processor it says is three times the last one, with two hundred and sixteen gigabytes of on-package memory and a cluster scaling to five hundred thousand cards. It is. And here's the date underneath it: mass production begins in the first quarter of twenty twenty-seven.
[pause] So nothing announced this week is in a rack this year.
Nothing. Twenty gigawatts of data centre is a twenty thirty-two number. The company published its own refutation.
What about the home lab — anything I could actually run?
The most downloaded text model on Hugging Face this week is twenty-seven billion parameters squeezed into just under six gigabytes.
Six? That fits on a laptop.
Weights constrained to minus one, zero and plus one. The vendor claims ninety-eight point two per cent of the full-precision benchmark average.
And is that true?
The benchmarks, yes. The behaviour, not quite. A user — not the vendor — measured it against the original and found it picks a different word about twenty-two per cent of the time.
[gasps] One word in five?
Roughly forty times the divergence of an ordinary four-bit version. And it isn't uniform — short maths and coding hold up, long agentic work falls over.
Did the vendor respond?
Partly, and fairly. They corrected their own comparison table the same day. Their claimed density lead dropped from two point three times to one point eight.
Credit for that. Anything else?
Stock inference software still can't load the file.
[laughs] Of course it can't.

The Kit, quickly. Meta announced VR Glasses on Tuesday. A hundred grams, five thousand pixels an eye, thirteen hundred dollars, shipping spring twenty twenty-seven. It is. And every reviewer led with the resolution, then a paragraph later with the field of view: seventy degrees by sixty-six.
Versus what on the older headset?
About a hundred and ten. One reviewer put it flatly — it feels far less immersive than a Quest once the light blockers go on.
So the headline number went up and the one that matters went down.
That's the issue in one sentence.
And the sceptic?

Forrester's own data is the harder problem. Seventy-six per cent of non-owners say they don't intend to buy smart glasses at all — and only twenty-one per cent said a camera-free version would change that.
[thoughtful] So the objection isn't the camera. It's the category.

Now — the Atelier. Coffee grinders, and this was the reader's own pick. The number on the box is burr diameter. The number that decides your cup is alignment — two hundredths of a millimetre. Two burrs are two planes. If they aren't parallel, the gap isn't a number, it's a wedge. One arc grinds at two hundred microns while the opposite arc grinds at three hundred and twenty. Every revolution. It blends two grind settings, and no dial removes it.
So bigger burrs don't help?
Here's the data. Jonathan Gagné measured three hundred particle-size distributions across twenty-four grinders. The idea that bigger flat burrs grind more uniformly is hearsay the data does not show.
[skeptical] So what am I paying four thousand dollars for?
Machining tolerance, workflow, service life, and an object. All real. None of them flavour.
Is there proof?
The best I've seen. A Swiss outfit tested twenty-four grinders from eighty euros to two thousand two hundred, then put the nine winners past a blind panel of two barista champions and two Q-graders.
And?

In the four-hundred-euro band, the cheapest single-dose grinder they knew brewed the best espresso in its group. The panel's favourites sat mid-field on uniformity, not at the extremes the advertising sells.
[laughs] So the champions couldn't rank them by price.
They could not.
One thing for a Singapore kitchen?

Humidity is on your side, and nobody says so. Static is what pins coffee fines to a chute wall, and static discharges readily in humid air — so the spray bottle everyone talks about matters far less here. The cost lands on storage instead. Roasted coffee is hygroscopic, so single-dose and seal the beans.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
What is it today?
Lapidary. Cutting gemstones.
[excited] Oh, I've wanted this one. Where's the deep end?
Four tribes: tumbling, cabbing, carving — and faceting. Cabbing is sculpture. Faceting is arithmetic you execute with your hands.
Meaning what, in practice?
A design is a table of angles and index positions. And there's a thing called a meetpoint, where three or more facet edges must converge on exactly one point.
And if you miss?
At ten times magnification they either meet or they visibly don't. It's binary. You can't smooth over it.
[thoughtful] No hiding.
The Guild president signs off his newsletter, without irony: may all of your meet points meet.
[laughs] That's lovely. Now the destruction — go on.

One cutter took forty point four carats of sapphire rough and finished with eleven. Another went thirty-five carats to fourteen and a half — two hundred and sixteen facets, two weeks. Always. And you can't see inside the rough when you buy it.
What does it cost to start?

This is the extraordinary part. The American establishment machines run from about four thousand to five thousand five hundred and ninety dollars. And a cheap imported base plus a fix-it kit comes to about five hundred and thirty.
[gasps] A ten-fold spread?

Inside one hobby, and it appeared in about three years. The kit-maker is refreshingly blunt — the cheap machines are almost functional out of the box, and their kit supplies everything missing, bar four things they can't ship.
Which are?
An alcohol lamp, lubricant spray, paper towels, and two buckets.
[laughs] Two buckets!
They've sold more than fifteen hundred kits.
And is the cheap rig any good?
The honest range runs from the quality is very poor, suitable for cheap jewellery, to a forum moderator who owns one saying he's seen very passable and even good stones cut on them.
And the best story in the whole desk?
A man rebuilt his cheap base with a digital angle encoder made from a thirty-dollar microcontroller and an industrial rotary sensor. Resolution: eighteen thousandths of a degree.
Better than the factory part?
Finer than the accessory the establishment sells for one thousand and eighty-five dollars.
[amused] And the chassis?
A cannibalised flat-pack step stool.
[laughs] Perfect. Absolutely perfect.
And here's what we didn't expect. Faceting is literally executing a numeric table of angles — the most computer-controllable task imaginable. So where's the automation?
Nowhere?

The canonical design software is free and asks for Windows ninety-five or later. The modern challenger's latest release is from December twenty nineteen. No hobby automated faceting machine has launched. The cutting edge here runs downward — price floor, modding, a microcontroller — not upward.
And Singapore?
No club at all. And that's the angle. The rough markets American cutters cross twelve time zones for are a long weekend from Changi — Chanthaburi is a ninety-minute flight, Sri Lanka four hours.
Can you do it in a flat?
Faceting, yes — it's a desk machine with a water drip. Cabbing, barely; it throws a fine stone slurry. Saws, no.
And the sceptic?

Brutal, and it comes from the community itself. Someone asked which discipline pays better per hour, and the answer was: you'll never sell them for what they're worth, time-wise. You can't compete with stones cut overseas.
[sighs] So don't quit your job.
The money, such as it is, is in cutting other people's stones to spec. And the best line wasn't about economics at all — when you make a job out of a hobby, it becomes a job, and you ruin the hobby.
[warmly] That's the truest thing you've read me all week.
Quickly, culture. A two-hander about a prisoner and his warden opened on fifteen hundred screens for two point three million dollars. Ninth place — and ninety-three per cent of critics.
What did they say?
One called it a future dad-movie classic, destined for a long afterlife of rewatches during Sunday afternoon recliner naps.
[laughs] I know exactly that film. And music?
A London jazz group went to number one on both the albums and the vinyl charts — the first British male jazz group with a number-one studio album.
Deserved?

Mostly rapturous. But the sharpest review says their instrumental prowess is buried beneath conventional structures, and that it feels like we are actually standing quite still. The chart measures reach, not risk. And fitness, where the number is twelve minutes. A hundred and forty-seven thousand adults, wrist-measured, nearly eight years of follow-up. A hundred and fifty minutes a week of moderate activity came with a thirty per cent lower mortality risk. And the same association was reached by about twelve minutes of vigorous activity.
[gasps] Twelve? That seems too good.

It might be. That's one week of wear on a wrist, years before anyone died. A separate paper this year found that correcting for measurement error changes the size of a comparable finding substantially. And the number is softer than it reads. Also, an accelerometer can't see resistance training at all.
Noted. And the family desk?
Three hundred and eleven eleven-to-fourteen-year-olds. Exam stress predicted compulsive social-media use — but almost entirely by way of restrictive parenting.
And supportive parenting?
Carried no effect either way. The pathway runs through restriction, not warmth.
[thoughtful] That's worth sitting with.

And so to the long read. Nepal. On the nineteenth of May, in offices in Kathmandu, a government committee paid out to ruined savers for the first time. Three hundred and seventy-eight people shared about one point four million rupees.
Which is how much each?
An average of three thousand seven hundred rupees. About twenty-four American dollars.
[whispers] Twenty-four dollars.
Against a claim of roughly forty-six billion rupees, owed to about seventy-six thousand depositors.
How did the money get there in the first place?

Nepal wrote the cooperative into its constitution as a pillar of the national economy. Seven point four million people joined — about one adult in four. Then the International Monetary Fund looked at it and produced the sentence that explains everything. These institutions were supervised, it wrote, by up to seven hundred and sixty-one different regulators.
[pause] Seven hundred and sixty-one. That's not a supervisory system.

It's a diagram of one. And the reason it existed matters. A third of Nepal's economy arrives every year as wages earned abroad, in the Gulf and Malaysia — landing in villages with no bank branch and no pension.
And the cooperative showed up.
Paying twelve to sixteen per cent. It wasn't a swindle that fooled people. It was the only answer to a question the formal system refused to answer.
So where did it go wrong?
Ask who can recruit twenty-five founding members in a Nepali ward. Ward chairs. Party operatives. Media owners. Members of parliament and their spouses.
So elite capture corrupted it.
No — and this is our argument. Elite capture didn't corrupt the cooperative. It was the distribution channel.
[exhales] That's a hard sentence.

And then it turns cruel in a way nobody counts. The money never stopped arriving — remittances hit the highest share of national income Nepal has ever recorded, and bank deposits grew nearly fourteen per cent.
And lending?
Total domestic credit grew two point one per cent.
So the money's just sitting there.
In Kathmandu, at two and three-quarter per cent. Kill the village bank and the deposits don't disappear — they migrate to the capital, and the village goes back to the moneylender.
And nobody's measuring that.
It appears in none of the forty-six billion.
Is anyone being held to account?

That's the third act, and an editor would refuse it as too neat in fiction. Nepal had a rising about elite capture last September; seventy-six people died. In March the party it produced won a hundred and eighty-two of two hundred and seventy-five seats.
And its chairman?
Is the country's most prominent cooperative-fraud defendant.
[whispers] Oh.
His government promised depositors under a hundred thousand rupees their money inside a hundred days.
And day one paid twenty-four dollars.
Day one paid twenty-four dollars.
Is this a banking crisis?
No, and we say so plainly. Cooperative deposits are about a twelfth of the banking system, and twenty-nine institutions were formally declared troubled out of roughly thirty-two thousand.
So it's not systemic.
It's a distributional catastrophe, not a financial-stability event. The political damage has already exceeded the financial. And we printed the hole in our own argument too.
Which is?
That the biggest named failures skew urban and Kathmandu, not village. Get the geography before you believe the sentence.
[thoughtful] And people saw this coming?

Six committees, between two thousand and four and twenty twenty-three, recommended in substance the same five things the Supreme Court ordered again in April. Nepal has known the answer for twenty-two years.
[sighs] That's the one that stays with me.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
